sizing.capsule_count_note: not in chip spec; sheet default 100,000 used

events.narration: Prime the board with oil before anything aqueous goes in. Do this first and always: the walls have to be oil-wetted for water-in-oil to work at all, and an aqueous stream that touches a dry wall first will wet it and keep wetting it.

Start the two aqueous streams. Cells ride in the core stream at about 310 cells/uL, which gives a mean of 0.2 cells per capsule. That figure belongs to a 135 um capsule and falls as the cube of diameter, so do not reuse it if the orifice changes.

Bring the oil up to rate and let the junction settle. Expect a minute or two of ragged, uneven droplets before it locks into a steady drip: that is normal, and it is the syringe pump and the tubing settling rather than the chip.

FILM THIS. At about 39 droplets per second the serpentine shows a regular train of 135 um capsules. Even spacing and even size is the whole result: if droplets vary in size the flow ratio is off, and if they merge the surfactant or the surface treatment is wrong.
Run for the demo batch: 5,000 capsules in about 2 min. A real run is ten times this and changes nothing about the chip.

Collect into a tube on ice. Let the two aqueous polymers demix for a few minutes, which is what puts the shell on the outside, then flood-cure at 405 nm. Curing is off-chip on purpose: demixing takes minutes, and a serpentine holding minutes at this flow would be longer than the board.
